summary: Specifies how a Binary Floor Control Protocol client connects to a floor control server outside of an offer/answer exchange. Authentication of client and server uses TLS. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: How a meeting participant connects to the person who decides who talks, with safe identity checks.

questions: how does a bfcp client connect to a server
subtitle: How a BFCP client connects to a floor control server when there is no SDP offer/answer to lean on, and how each side proves who it is.

tldr.problem: A client of the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) needs to open a connection to a floor control server, but outside an SDP offer/answer exchange there is no protected channel for swapping certificate fingerprints.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens a TCP connection and runs TLS over it. The server always acts as the TLS server and proves its identity with a certificate, while the client proves itself with a pre-shared secret using PSK-TLS.
tldr.outcome: BFCP connections made outside offer/answer get a defined way to connect, reconnect and authenticate both ends. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5018 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Connecting Outside Offer/Answer
sections.content:
The Binary Floor Control Protocol (RFC 4582) lets conference participants ask a floor control server for permission to use a shared resource. To start, a client needs the server's transport address, the conference identifier and the user identifier. RFC 4583 covers how to connect when these are exchanged in an SDP offer/answer exchange. RFC 5018 covers every other case.

The difference matters for security. An offer/answer exchange gives both parties an initial integrity-protected channel, which they can use to swap fingerprints of self-signed certificates. Outside that model, such a channel is not typically available. So this RFC picks a different pair of mechanisms: PSK-TLS to authenticate clients and server certificates to authenticate servers.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you can agree on a secret handshake ahead of time, and sometimes you cannot. This RFC is for when you cannot, so it uses a different way to check identities.

sections.title: Opening and Reopening the TCP Connection
sections.content:
How the client learns the server address, the conference identifier and the user identifier is out of scope. The RFC assumes an out-of-band method. Once the client has the server's IP address and port, it performs an active TCP open towards it.

If the client has only a host name, it MUST do a DNS lookup first, using an A or AAAA lookup (or both). IPv6-only or dual-stack clients MUST use name resolution functions that implement the address selection algorithms of RFC 3484, which produce an ordered list of IPv6 and IPv4 destination addresses. The RFC warns that these algorithms depend on broad operating system support, and points developers to RFC 4943 for address resolution delays. A list that starts with unusable IPv6 global addresses can delay completing the connection.

RFC 4582 lists situations where the connection must be reestablished but does not say how, because that depends on how it was first made. This RFC fills the gap: when the TCP connection is closed following the RFC 4582 rules, the client SHOULD reestablish it. If a TCP connection cannot deliver a BFCP message and times out, the client SHOULD also reestablish it.
sections.eli5: The client calls the server's phone number. If it only knows a name, it looks the number up first. If the call drops, it calls again.

sections.title: TLS Usage
sections.content:
RFC 4582 requires every BFCP entity to implement TLS and recommends using it on all connections. TLS gives integrity and replay protection and, optionally, confidentiality. This RFC adds one fixed role: the floor control server MUST always act as the TLS server.

If a floor control server receives a BFCP message over plain TCP, with no TLS, it SHOULD ask for TLS by sending an Error message with an Error code of 9 (Use TLS).
sections.eli5: TLS is a sealed, tamper-proof envelope. The server always plays the part of the one who owns the mailbox, and if you send it an open postcard it tells you to use an envelope.

sections.title: Authenticating Server and Client
sections.content:
BFCP supports server authentication with certificates and client authentication with a pre-shared secret.

For the server, the floor control server MUST present its certificate during TLS setup. The certificate MUST either be signed directly by one of the other party's trust anchors or be validated through a certification path ending at one. If the client knows the server's host name, it MUST check it against the identity in the certificate, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. A subjectAltName extension of type dNSName, when present, MUST be used as the identity. Otherwise the most specific Common Name in the Subject is used, which is deprecated. Common Name matching allows a wildcard character that matches any single domain name component or fragment, so a name that is a star followed by .a.com matches foo.a.com but not bar.foo.a.com. If the client only knows an IP address, an iPAddress subjectAltName must be present and must exactly match it.

On a mismatch, a user-oriented client MUST either notify the user or terminate the connection with a bad certificate error. An automated client MUST log the error to an audit log if one is available and SHOULD terminate the connection. Automated clients MAY offer a setting that turns this check off, but MUST provide a setting that turns it on.

For the client, authentication is based on a pre-shared secret using PSK-TLS (RFC 4279). The BFCP specification already mandates the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA ciphersuite. Clients and servers following this RFC MUST also support TLS_RSA_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.
sections.eli5: The server shows an ID card from an office you trust, and you check the name on it. You show the secret password you both agreed on earlier. Now each of you knows the other is real.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because authentication relies on TLS, it is strongly RECOMMENDED to always use TLS with non-null encryption. Other security mechanisms are allowed if they give similar properties: replay and integrity protection, confidentiality, and client and server authentication.

The main caveat is the pre-shared key. When keys come from text passwords, PSK mode is open to offline dictionary attacks. So clients should, where possible, use certificate-based server authentication ciphersuites with password-derived keys. Passwords SHOULD have enough entropy: at least 8 characters from a mixed pool, with the RFC noting an 8-character ASCII password has a maximum entropy of 56 bits and generally far lower. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to support at least 16-character passwords or passphrases, and MAY derive the key from a passphrase with a function such as PBKDF2. Randomly generated keys defeat dictionary attacks; they SHOULD come from a strong random number generator, with a minimum length of 80 bits.

The RFC also walks through four threats. Impersonating a client, to forge or grant floor requests, is blocked by TLS. Impersonating a server, to make clients think they hold a floor, is blocked by the server certificate. Modifying messages is blocked by TLS integrity protection. Eavesdropping on details such as why a request was denied is blocked by TLS confidentiality, which is why non-null encryption is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A short, guessable password is easy for a sneaky guesser to crack, so pick a long one. Using the sealed envelope and the ID card stops people from pretending, changing notes or reading them.
